clue.text: Bookmaker, old Indian's savoury filling

indicators.note: the filling of a pastry is its inside, so the outer letters of the snack are shed

parts.note: a samosa is a fried Indian pastry snack

explanation.surface: A bookie tucks into an Indian snack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bookmaker' is not a bookie here: it is the prophet whose name heads a book of the Old Testament. 'Filling' keeps only the inside of SAMOSA.
explanation.definitionFit: The prophet Amos gave his name to a book of the Bible, so he is a maker of a book.

clue.text: Master Valentine's given this language

parts.note: to master a machine is to man it; also man as in 'man and master'
a valentine card is signed with a kiss, written X

explanation.surface: A schoolmaster's sweetheart receives a message in a foreign tongue.
explanation.definitionFit: Manx is the Celtic tongue of the Isle of Man, revived after its last native speaker died.

clue.text: Be the jester, who in Marseille has prankster's hat

parts.note: qui is French for who, Marseille being a French city

indicators.note: a hat sits on top, so this takes the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A French jester wonders whose cap belongs to the joker.
explanation.definitionFit: To make a witty remark is to play the jester; the verb sense of a witticism.

clue.text: Relax for a while, then rela…

parts.note: the truncated word is relax with its X, the Roman numeral for ten, removed, so the instruction that produces it is the answer

explanation.surface: An instruction to relax that trails off before it finishes, as if the speaker dozed.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half is a reverse clue: X is the Roman numeral for ten, and taking it from RELAX leaves the printed 'rela…'.
explanation.definitionFit: To take a ten-minute break is an idiom for pausing and resting briefly.

clue.text: See 13
One wants kinky clue to accompaniment — but that isn't required here!

definitions.text: One wants kinky clue to accompaniment — but that isn't required here!

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: kinky means twisted, so the following words are bent into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone craves a racy clue to go with something, yet the clue says a partner is not needed.
explanation.walkthrough: I (One) followed by a rearrangement of CLUE TO ACCOMPANIMENT gives the whole phrase. Read as a whole, the clue says that this is a conception needing no partner.
explanation.definitionFit: The doctrine concerns a birth without sin, popularly taken as one where no partner was needed, so a companion is not required.

clue.text: A bloomer, blowing up before end of England tie?

indicators.note: something blown up is shattered, so the letters are reassembled
only the part of the word before its end is used, dropping its last letter

explanation.surface: A cricket blunder that blows up just before England's drawn match ends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before end of' trims England to ENGLAN; 'blowing up' rearranges ENGLAN with TIE.
explanation.definitionFit: Eglantine is the sweet briar, a wild rose, so it is a flowering plant: a bloomer.

clue.text: The sound emanating from Barker explains our deserting Court Four

parts.note: to court a lover is to woo

indicators.note: deserting means leaving, so these letters leave the word four

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A tennis player called Barker explains that their side has left Court Four.
explanation.walkthrough: Barker reads as a name but is simply a dog.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog's bark is the noise written as this sound, so it is what comes out of any barker.

clue.text: Nasty hitch interrupts fantastic bun being baked

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break into, so this group sits inside the other word

parts.note: a wild idea is a fantastic one

indicators.note: something nasty is twisted, so the letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A baker's mishap breaks up a fanciful bun while it is in the oven.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nasty' and 'interrupts' look like part of the baking story. The definition plays on the British idiom 'a bun in the oven', meaning expecting a baby.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a bun in the oven is British slang for being pregnant, so a bun being baked means an expected baby.

clue.text: The reversal of truces changes it

indicators.note: the reversal of a word reads it from the back, so the Latin plural is turned round

parts.note: pax is Latin for peace or truce, so the plural is paxes
in bell-ringing a peal is a set of changes rung on the bells

explanation.surface: Peace treaties torn up alter everything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The reversal of' turns PAXES to SEXAP. 'It' is old slang for allure, from Clara Bow, the 'It girl'.
explanation.definitionFit: It as a noun is dated slang for physical attractiveness, the quality that draws people in.

clue.text: The first of my previous wives turns up … with one?

definitions.text: The first of my previous wives turns up … with one?

parts.note: a means one

indicators.note: in a down entry turning up reads the letters from the bottom

parts.words: The first of my previous wives
parts.note: an ex is a former wife

explanation.surface: A former wife arrives carrying something sinister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turns up' does double duty: it reverses the former wife, and in the whole picture she arrives armed, with a hint of Henry VIII's wives.
explanation.definitionFit: A vengeful former spouse might arrive carrying a chopping tool, and the clue as a whole describes that.

clue.text: Go direct, and change result

definitions.meaning: a go in a game is one's chance to play
to direct one's attention is to point it somewhere
to alter how something comes out, as a match or milk can go sour

explanation.surface: A coach tells a player to take control and alter the outcome.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers a player's go, pointing something in a direction, and a game's reversal of fortune.

clue.text: Carmen? It's the intro of harp that is so lovely!

parts.note: read as car men, the motoring organisation AA, the Automobile Association

indicators.note: an intro is the opening of a piece, so the first letter is used

explanation.surface: An opera fan hears the harp open Carmen and sighs with delight.
explanation.walkthrough: Carmen looks like Bizet's opera; split it as car men, the British breakdown service known as the AA.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an exclamation of contented pleasure, the noise one makes at something delightful.

clue.text: Do without anagram of lace, following compiler's own

indicators.note: without in the old sense of outside, so the swindle wraps around the rest

parts.note: to do someone is to cheat or con them

indicators.note: following puts the rearranged letters after the compiler

parts.note: the compiler refers to himself as me

indicators.note: the setter openly names the device: the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A setter plans to manage without a word puzzle of lace, after his own clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' is used in its old sense of outside, and 'Do' is a verb meaning cheat. The setter names the device openly with 'anagram of'.
explanation.definitionFit: To own up is to admit, and own alone means confess; both match the idiom for telling the truth.

clue.text: Press into paying exorbitantly for this

definitions.text: Press into paying exorbitantly for this

parts.words: Press into paying exorbitantly for this
parts.note: the press, newspapers, paying huge sums for exclusive stories; press into also suggests coercing

explanation.surface: Someone is forced to pay a fortune for something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press' reads as a verb, to coerce, but it is the newspapers, who pay big sums for a story.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the tabloid practice of buying exclusive stories from sources for large sums.

clue.text: £500 a head for something to eat

parts.note: a monkey is British slang for five hundred pounds
nut is slang for the head

explanation.surface: A restaurant charges five hundred pounds per person for a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: '£500 a head' looks like a menu price; MONKEY is British slang for £500 and NUT is slang for a head.
explanation.definitionFit: The peanut is also called by this name, an edible seed eaten as a snack.

clue.text: Risk reduced, sheikh's clamped wheels

indicators.note: clamped means gripped, so the shortened word holds the other one inside
reduced means cut short, so the last letter goes

parts.note: to chance something is to risk it
a sheikh is an Arab leader; the 's stands for has

explanation.surface: A sheikh's car gets clamped, cutting down the risk of it being driven off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clamped' looks like a parking penalty but is the container signal, and 'wheels' is slang for a vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: A charabanc is an old open motor coach for outings, and wheels is slang for a vehicle.

clue.text: Oik playing havoc, wasting oxygen

indicators.note: playing about with letters means rearranging them
wasting means losing, so the element's symbol is lost

parts.note: O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: A lout causing chaos while breathing heavily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wasting' takes O from HAVOC, leaving HAVC; 'playing' rearranges it. CHAV is British slang for a brash, loutish youth.
explanation.definitionFit: Oik is British slang for a coarse, ill-mannered person, a close synonym for a young lout.

clue.text: No Scots heading back into overnight accommodation with silver cushion

indicators.note: into means going inside, so the reversed word sits within the lodging

parts.note: B and B, bed and breakfast

indicators.note: heading back means going backwards, so the Scots word is read in reverse

parts.note: nae is Scots for no
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: A Scot heads back to a guesthouse with a silver cushion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heading back' turns NAE into EAN, which goes 'into' BB, short for bed and breakfast.
explanation.definitionFit: A beanbag is a large soft bag of beads used as a floor seat, so a cushion of sorts.

clue.text: Car hits edge of kerb — hip affected

parts.note: the Mini is a small British car

indicators.note: the edge here is the front end of the word, its first letter

parts.note: hip and in both mean fashionable

explanation.surface: A car mounts the kerb and someone's hip is hurt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Affected' looks like injured, but it means pretentious, the adjective sense of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Minikin as an adjective means dainty or mincing, so it describes an affected, prissy manner.

clue.text: Operatic duo surveying part of Hertfordshire strip, covering little

indicators.note: surveying means looking down on, so in a down entry this pair sits above the town

parts.note: G and S, Gilbert and Sullivan, writers of comic operas
Tring is a town in Hertfordshire, a county north of London

explanation.surface: Gilbert and Sullivan inspect a strip of land in Hertfordshire.
explanation.walkthrough: TRING is a small town in Hertfordshire, the English county just north of London.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny garment of a narrow band of cloth, worn by strippers, that covers very little.

clue.text: Nothing on? Crocodile Dundee will entertain over

indicators.note: over means turned over, so the run of letters is read backwards
to entertain is to hold within, so the letters lie inside these words

explanation.surface: Is anything on TV? Crocodile Dundee will provide entertainment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Will entertain' points to letters inside CROCODILE DUNDEE, and 'over' reads them backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Wearing nothing on means being without clothes, which is the adjective's sense.

clue.text: Son turns head, meeting mum here? …

indicators.note: meeting joins the two pieces side by side
the head of the word, its first two letters, is turned round

parts.note: Master is a title for a young son, as in Master Tom
a dam is a mother, of an animal

explanation.surface: A boy turns his head and meets his mother somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: Master is the old courtesy title for a boy, so it stands for 'Son'. 'Here?' is fair because the city's name ends in a dam.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dutch capital is built around a dam, so a mother called a dam would be at home in it.

clue.text: Letter delivered to Manor House

indicators.note: a letter delivered to an address ends up inside it, so the letters lie within these words

explanation.surface: The post arrives at a country manor.
explanation.definitionFit: Rho is the seventeenth character of the Greek alphabet, so a letter.

clue.text: … and facing the other way completely — rough!

indicators.note: facing fully the other way means the whole word is read backwards

parts.note: the ellipsis carries over Son from the previous clue, and a son is a boy

explanation.surface: A child completely turned around, with a rough manner.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis carries 'Son' over from the previous clue; this time the whole word is turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: A yob is a rough lout, so the noun suits a rough as in a ruffian.

clue.text: Here in Scotland anything goes?

parts.note: when anything goes there is a nil ban, nothing forbidden: O, zero
the ban that is nil, a prohibition

explanation.surface: A Scottish place where everything is permitted?
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'anything goes' as zero prohibition: O for nought plus BAN. OBAN is a port town on Scotland's west coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Oban is a coastal town in Argyll, so a place in Scotland, which the clue calls here.

clue.text: Killer repulsed with refinement: not hard in citadel

indicators.note: repulsed means driven back, so the whale is read backwards

parts.note: the orca is the killer whale

indicators.note: not hard means take away H, the pencil grading for hard

parts.note: polish is elegance or refinement

explanation.surface: A murderer is driven off by good manners, in a soft fashion, inside a fortress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Repulsed' turns ORCA to ACRO; 'not hard' drops H from POLISH.
explanation.definitionFit: An acropolis is the fortified upper part of an ancient Greek city, its citadel.

clue.text: Compilers heading back to pub that was very close!

indicators.note: to means added onto, so the reversed pair is placed after the pub

parts.note: PH is short for public house

indicators.note: heading back means going in reverse, so the pair is read backwards

parts.note: setters refer to themselves as we

explanation.surface: Crossword setters dash back to the pub after a near miss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heading back' reverses WE to EW, which goes 'to' PH.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an exclamation of relief after a narrow escape or a near thing.

clue.text: Jump about zone, following topless lady of the night

indicators.note: following puts the zone letter after the other piece
topless means losing the top, the first letter in a down entry

parts.note: a slut is a derogatory term for a promiscuous woman, here a prostitute

explanation.surface: A topless prostitute leaps around the area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topless' drops the S of SLUT, and Z comes after.
explanation.definitionFit: The lutz is a figure-skating leap taking off from the back outside edge of a skate.

clue.text: Silence love with exposure

parts.note: sh is an order to keep quiet
love is zero in tennis, O

explanation.surface: Someone hushes up a love affair as it threatens to be exposed.
explanation.definitionFit: A show is a display or public airing, a putting on view.

clue.text: Brown bread, last of ashes disposed perfectly

indicators.note: disposed of means got rid of, so this letter is taken out

parts.note: toast is bread browned under heat

indicators.note: this takes the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone dead and cremated, with the ashes neatly scattered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brown bread' is Cockney rhyming slang for dead, a false trail with ashes; here it is toast. 'Disposed' drops the S from 'last of ashes'.
explanation.definitionFit: To a T is an idiom meaning exactly or perfectly, fitting precisely.
